title: Short-Term vs Long-Term Rental
keyLine: One is a small hotel. One is a lease. Tax rules follow the stay length and your hours, not the brand of the app.
description: STR vs long-term rental in plain words: work, cash, and the IRS 7-day average stay test. No invented occupancy. Calculators and W-2 notes included.
answer: A long-term rental is a home you lease for months at a time, often a year. A short-term rental (STR) is a stay measured in nights, often listed on Airbnb or Vrbo. STR usually means more guest work, more furniture, and more local rules. Long-term usually means a steadier lease and fewer turnovers. Tax is a separate test. IRS Publication 925 says an activity is not a 'rental activity' for passive-loss rules if the average stay is 7 days or less. You still have to materially participate. This page does not promise a tax save.

blocks.heading: The 7-day test, in plain words
paragraphs: [IRS Publication 925](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p925) says an activity is not treated as a rental activity if the average period of customer use is 7 days or less. You figure that average by dividing total days in all rental periods by the number of rentals for the year.

Clearing 7 days does not make losses deductible. You still need material participation, which is a separate hour-and-facts test in the same publication. A full-time W-2 job makes some of those tests hard. A spouse's hours can matter on a joint return. That is facts, not a loophole slogan.

Long-term residential leases usually stay in the rental-activity bucket. Losses are often passive unless you qualify as a real estate professional. That status needs more than 750 hours and more than half of your working time in real property trades. A full-time job usually blocks the second half. Details: [REPS vs STR loophole](/compare/real-estate-professional-vs-str-loophole).

blocks.heading: How to compare dollars without a fantasy spreadsheet
paragraphs: Use two tools on the same property idea. [Rental cash flow](/tools/rental-property-cash-flow) for a yearly lease. [STR break-even occupancy](/tools/str-break-even-occupancy) for a nightly model. Do not copy someone else's occupancy. Use a conservative number you can defend.

Add cleaning, supplies, furniture replacement, and permit fees to the STR side. Add vacancy and repairs to both. Then ask whether you will do the work. A prettier STR net that needs you every weekend is not passive.

blocks.label: W-2 readers
paragraphs: Do not buy an STR because a class said it 'unlocks depreciation on wages.' Read [the short-term rental loophole guide](/tax-strategies/short-term-rental-loophole) and talk to a CPA. Depreciation can reverse when you sell. See our recapture guide if you go that far.

faqs.a: No. Higher nightly rates can lose after cleaning, vacancy, and furniture. Run both models. We will not quote a typical occupancy because we do not have your city data.

faqs.q: Does a 7-day average stay cut my W-2 tax?
faqs.a: Not by itself. It can change whether the activity is a rental for passive-loss rules. You still need material participation and a real property. Ask a CPA.

faqs.q: Can I switch from STR to long-term mid year?
faqs.a: Operations yes, if the law allows. The average-stay math for that tax year can get messy if long stays mix with short stays. Publication 925 is the starting text. Then a CPA.
